newsitem.title: UK: Angry farmers lobby UK Conservatives on cow cull.
newsitem.headline: Angry farmers lobby UK Conservatives on cow cull.

text.p: Hundreds of angry beef farmers descended on the annual conference of Britain's ruling Conservative Party on Tuesday to vent their anger over a mad cow crisis which they say is threatening their business.
As their leaders held an 80-minute meeting with Prime Minister John Major, farmers barracked delegates and members of parliament waving placards which said: "The government is mad, not our cows".
Farmers are furious about government plans to slaughter thousands of cattle, a move the European Union demanded in exchange for gradually lifting a ban on British beef exports.
The ban, imposed after evidence that Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) could be transmitted to humans, has hit the beef industry hard.
The farmers' protest highlighted a potent threat to the Conservatives in rural areas they regard as providing the backbone of their parliamentary party.
Major and Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg did what they could to placate the demonstrators.
Speaking after his meeting with National Farmers Union President Sir David Naish, Major said he "understood and sympathised" with the farmers.
"I make no promise that we can rub away all the bruises, but I very much want to work with the industry," he said.
Hogg, in his keynote speech to the conference on Tuesday, announced a 45 million pound ($70 million) package of measures to help the industry.
Naish welcomed the extra cash but said the government had to ensure farmers received the money as soon as possible.
Hogg also said there was no point in slaughtering extra cattle to eradicate BSE, making clear he would not yield to EU demands for an extra cull of up to 147,000 cows.

"By the turn of this century, 2001 or thereabouts, BSE will largely have disappeared from the national herd. There is no credible cull policy which will substantially accelerate the rate of decline or materially bring forward the date when it is totally eradicated," Hogg told delegates.
Britain's refusal to go along with the extra cull -- which it agreed to in June talks with the EU -- has dashed the prospects of the export ban being lifted in the near future.
